title: Question 2
stem: A person uses a trolley to move suitcases at an airport. The total mass of the trolley and suitcases is $72\text{ kg}$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: The person pushes the trolley and suitcases along a horizontal surface with a constant speed of $1.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and then releases the trolley. The released trolley moves in a straight line and comes to rest. Assume that a constant total resistive force of $18\text{ N}$ opposes the motion of the trolley and suitcases.
parts.text: Calculate the power required to overcome the total resistive force on the trolley and suitcases when they move with a constant speed of $1.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what it means to push at constant speed - your push must exactly balance the 18 N resistive force, so what steady force are you providing?
Hint 2: Recall how power links that steady force to the speed, then multiply the 18 N force by the 1.4 m s-1 speed to get power in watts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Constant Speed Pushing**
You are walking with the trolley at a steady $1.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Steady speed means no resultant force, so your forward push must equal the backward resistive force of $18\text{ N}$.

Step 2: **Use Power = Force x Velocity**
Power is the rate of doing work against resistance:
$$P = Fv$$
$$P = 18 \times 1.4 = 25.2\text{ W} \approx 25\text{ W}$$

Power is the rate of doing work against resistance:

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the trolley to come to rest after it is released.
hints: Hint 1: After release, only the 18 N resistive force acts, so the trolley must slow down - which law links this unbalanced force to the mass and deceleration?
Hint 2: Use $F = ma$ with $F = 18\text{ N}$ and $m = 72\text{ kg}$ to find the size of the deceleration.
Hint 3: Link the starting speed of 1.4 m s-1 and final speed of zero to that deceleration to find the stopping time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find The Deceleration After Release**
Once you let go, the only horizontal force is the $18\text{ N}$ resistance backwards. It causes a deceleration given by Newton's second law:
$$a = \frac{F}{m}$$
$$a = \frac{18}{72} = 0.25\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Step 2: **Convert Slowing To Time**
The trolley starts at $u = 1.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and ends at $v = 0$. For uniform deceleration:
$$v = u - at$$
$$0 = 1.4 - 0.25t$$

Step 3: **Calculate The Stopping Time**
$$t = \frac{1.4}{0.25} = 5.6\text{ s}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
At another place in the airport, the trolley and suitcases are on a slope, as shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1 (not to scale)

The person releases the trolley from rest at point $X$. The trolley moves down the slope in a straight line towards point $Y$. The distance along the slope between points $X$ and $Y$ is $9.5\text{ m}$.

The component $F$ of the weight of the trolley and suitcases that acts along the slope is $54\text{ N}$. Assume that a constant total resistive force of $18\text{ N}$ opposes the motion of the trolley and suitcases.
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the trolley at point $Y$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 2.1 - one component pulls the trolley down the slope while resistance pulls back up, so what is the net force down the slope?
Hint 2: Use that net force and the 72 kg mass to find the acceleration down the 9.5 m slope.
Hint 3: The trolley starts from rest, so choose a kinematic equation linking acceleration, distance 9.5 m and final speed v with u = 0.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get The Resultant Force Down The Slope**
Down the slope you have $F = 54\text{ N}$ from weight, up the slope you have $18\text{ N}$ resistance. The resultant is:
$$F_{net} = 54 - 18 = 36\text{ N down the slope}$$

Step 2: **Find The Acceleration**
Apply $F = ma$:
$$a = \frac{36}{72} = 0.50\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Step 3: **Use Kinematics Over 9.5 m**
Start from rest, so $u = 0$, $s = 9.5\text{ m}$:
$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$
$$v^2 = 0 + 2 \times 0.50 \times 9.5 = 9.5$$
$$v = \sqrt{9.5} \approx 3.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the work done by $F$ for the movement of the trolley from $X$ to $Y$.
hints: Hint 1: Remember work done by a constant force is force times distance moved in the direction of that force - which force and which distance apply for F here?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Work = Force x Distance**
Force $F = 54\text{ N}$ acts all the way along the $9.5\text{ m}$ from X to Y:
$$W = Fs$$
$$W = 54 \times 9.5 = 513\text{ J} \approx 510\text{ J}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The trolley is released at point $X$ at time $t = 0$.

On Fig. 2.2, sketch a graph to show the variation with time $t$ of the work done by $F$ for the movement of the trolley from $X$ to $Y$. Numerical values of the work done and $t$ are not required.

{{figure:figure_2_2}}

Fig. 2.2
hints: Hint 1: Start at the origin since zero time means zero distance moved and zero work, then think about whether the trolley moves at steady speed or gets faster.
Hint 2: Think about how the rate of doing work (power = F x v) changes as v grows, and what that means for the gradient of a work against time graph.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at origin with increasing gradient (steeper with time) as speed and rate of work increase.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start At The Origin**
At $t = 0$ the trolley has just been released at X, so no distance has been covered and work done by $F$ is zero. Your line must start at (0,0).

Step 2: **Show An Increasing Gradient**
The trolley accelerates, so in each extra second it travels further and $F$ does more work. Power $P = Fv$ grows because $v$ grows. Since gradient of work-time graph = power, the gradient must increase. Draw a smooth upward-curving line, getting steeper with $t$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The angle of the slope in (b) is constant. The frictional forces acting on the wheels of the moving trolley are also constant.

Explain why, in practice, it is incorrect to assume that the total resistive force opposing the motion of the trolley and suitcases is constant as the trolley moves between $X$ and $Y$.

markscheme_points.text: (force due to) air resistance increases/changes/not constant or air

hints: Hint 1: The slope angle and wheel friction are fixed, but what other part of the total resistance depends on how fast the air is rushing past the trolley?
parts.proper_answer: Air resistance (drag) increases as speed increases, so total resistive force is not constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot The Speed-Dependent Force**
Total resistance is wheel friction plus air resistance. Wheel friction can stay roughly constant, but air drag gets larger when the trolley moves faster. As the trolley accelerates from X to Y, its speed rises from zero to about $3.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$, so air resistance grows and the assumption of a constant $18\text{ N}$ total is incorrect in practice.
